front: Who can act as importer of record (IOR) on a US entry?
back: The owner or purchaser of the goods, or a licensed customs broker designated by the owner, purchaser or consignee (19 U.S.C. 1484).

front: What is a licensed customs broker?
back: A person or company licensed by the customs authority to transact customs business for importers: preparing and filing entries, paying duties and dealing with customs. US brokers are licensed by CBP under 19 CFR Part 111.

front: If our broker files and pays a US entry, who remains liable for the duties?
back: The importer. Duties are its personal debt to the US (19 CFR 141.1(b)), and paying the broker does not discharge it if the broker fails to pay CBP.

front: What is CBP's role in US imports?
back: U.S. Customs and Border Protection (part of DHS) releases goods, assesses and collects duties, taxes and fees, enforces trade laws, fixes final classification and value at liquidation, and operates ACE.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 2

front: What is the CBSA's role in Canadian imports?
back: The Canada Border Services Agency releases imported goods, assesses and collects duties and taxes (including GST) through CARM, enforces border and trade laws, and licenses customs brokers.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 2

front: How do ANAM and SAT divide responsibilities for Mexican imports?
back: ANAM (Agencia Nacional de Aduanas de México, operating since 1 Jan 2022 under SHCP) runs customs and collects foreign-trade duties. SAT remains the tax authority: RFC, e.firma, padrón de importadores and domestic taxes.

front: What is an agente aduanal?
back: A Mexican customs broker: an individual holding a government-issued patente who prepares and files pedimentos and clears goods on the importer's behalf. Broker firms are called agencias aduanales.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.1

front: Why does our team audit what brokers file if brokers are licensed experts?
back: Because in all three countries the importer, not the broker, stays responsible for accurate declarations and duties. We supply the classification, value and origin data, so we must verify brokers declared it correctly.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 1

front: What is the difference between a US entry and an entry summary?
back: The entry (cargo release, CBP Form 3461 data) asks CBP to release the goods. The entry summary (CBP Form 7501 data) declares classification, value and origin and deposits estimated duties. They can be filed together.

front: When is a US entry summary due if it is not filed at the time of entry?
back: Within 10 working days after the time of entry, with estimated duties attached (19 CFR 142.12(b)).

front: What does US entry type 01 mean?
back: Consumption entry, free and dutiable: the standard formal entry for commercial goods entering US commerce.

front: What does US entry type 11 mean?
back: Informal entry, free and dutiable: a simplified entry for low-value shipments, generally US$2,500 or less (19 CFR 143.21). Quota and AD/CVD goods need formal entry; Chapter 99 goods have a separate, lower limit (as of Oct 2026)

front: Under 19 CFR 143.21(a), what informal-entry limit applies to goods classified in HTSUS Chapter 99, Subchapters III and IV?
back: US$250, not the general US$2,500. Additional duties such as Sections 232 and 301 are reported in Chapter 99, so most tariffed shipments over US$250 need formal entry (CBP confirmed, March 2025).

front: What is ACE?
back: The Automated Commercial Environment: CBP's single-window system for processing US imports and exports. Brokers file entries into it, and importers can run reports on their own entries in the ACE Portal.

front: What is ABI?
back: The Automated Broker Interface: the electronic (EDI) channel that brokers and self-filing importers use to transmit entries and entry summaries into ACE, built to CBP's CATAIR specifications.

front: What is liquidation of a US entry?
back: CBP's final computation (ascertainment) of the duties, taxes and fees owed on an entry. After liquidation, changes generally need a protest rather than a post-summary correction.

front: When do most US entries liquidate in practice?
back: About 314 days after the date of entry: ACE schedules automatic liquidation then unless liquidation is extended or suspended. Check the actual scheduled date in ACE (as of Oct 2026)
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 4.2

front: What is the statutory deadline for CBP to liquidate a US entry?
back: One year from the date of entry (19 U.S.C. 1504), extendable to a maximum of four years. If CBP misses it, the entry is deemed liquidated at the rate, value and amount the importer declared.

front: What is a Post-Summary Correction (PSC)?
back: An electronic correction to an accepted, unliquidated entry summary, filed through ACE, e.g., to fix classification, value or a preference claim. It can increase or decrease the duty owed.

front: What is the filing window for a Post-Summary Correction?
back: Within 300 days from the date of entry and no later than 15 days before the scheduled liquidation date, whichever is earlier. After liquidation, use a protest or prior disclosure instead.

front: How long does an importer have to file a US protest?
back: 180 days after the date of liquidation (or of the decision protested) for entries made on or after 18 Dec 2004 (19 CFR 174.12). File in ACE or on CBP Form 19.

front: What does reasonable care require of a US importer?
back: A legal duty (19 U.S.C. 1484, from the 1993 Mod Act) to use care in entering, classifying and valuing goods and giving CBP accurate information. Relying on a broker does not transfer this duty.

front: What is a US prior disclosure?
back: Telling CBP about a customs violation (19 U.S.C. 1592) before, or without knowledge of, a formal investigation, and paying the lost duties. It substantially reduces penalties (19 CFR 162.74).

front: What is a US customs bond?
back: A surety contract guaranteeing CBP that duties, taxes and fees will be paid and entry obligations met. A single transaction bond covers one entry; a continuous bond covers all entries for a year and renews.

front: What is ISF '10+2'?
back: Importer Security Filing for US-bound ocean cargo: the importer files 10 data elements (e.g., seller, buyer, manufacturer, country of origin, HTS-6) at least 24 hours before lading abroad; the carrier files 2 (stow plan, container status messages).

front: How long must US import records be kept?
back: Generally five years from the date of entry (19 CFR 163.4). More specific rules control where they exist; e.g., drawback records are kept until 3 years after the drawback claim is liquidated (19 CFR 190.15).

front: How long must Canadian import records be kept?
back: Six years following the importation of commercial goods, normally at the importer's place of business in Canada (Imported Goods Records Regulations; CBSA Memorandum D17-1-21).

front: How long must Mexican import records generally be kept?
back: Generally five years: the Código Fiscal de la Federación (art. 30) sets five years and defers to customs law for import documents. Program-specific rules (e.g., IMMEX) can differ; the Senior confirms them.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 3.4

front: How long must an importer claiming USMCA preference keep records?
back: At least five years from the date of importation, including the certification of origin relied on (USMCA Art. 5.8). National law can require longer, e.g., Canada's six years.

front: What is the primary customs valuation method in the US, Canada and Mexico?
back: Transaction value: the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the importing country, plus specified additions. All three follow the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 9.1

front: What are the five statutory additions to US transaction value?
back: If not already in the price: packing costs, selling commissions paid by the buyer, assists, royalties or license fees paid as a condition of sale, and resale proceeds accruing to the seller.

front: What is an assist in customs valuation?
back: Something the buyer supplies free or at reduced cost for producing the imported goods: materials or components, tools/dies/molds, merchandise consumed in production, or engineering/design work done outside the US (19 CFR 152.102).

front: Why are assists a data risk for a BSA?
back: Their value must be added to the declared customs value, but they rarely appear on the supplier invoice or PO (e.g., molds we paid for), so value data built only from purchase prices understates value.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 9.3

front: Which costs are excluded from US transaction value if separately identified?
back: International freight and insurance to the US; post-importation construction, assembly, maintenance or technical assistance; transportation after importation; and US duties and federal taxes owed because of importation (19 CFR 152.103).

front: Which of the three countries values imports on a CIF basis?
back: Mexico: customs value includes freight, insurance and related costs up to the point of entry. The US excludes international freight; Canada excludes transport from the place of direct shipment to Canada.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Sections 3.3 and 9.3

front: Can transaction value be used for related-party purchases?
back: Yes, if the relationship did not influence the price (shown by the circumstances of sale) or the price closely approximates a test value. The importer must be able to show this.

front: What is an ad valorem duty?
back: A duty charged as a percentage of the goods' customs value, e.g., X% of value.

front: What is a specific duty?
back: A duty charged per physical unit, e.g., cents per kilogram, per dozen or per liter, regardless of the goods' value.

front: What is a compound duty?
back: A duty that combines an ad valorem and a specific component on the same tariff line, e.g., X% of value plus Y cents per kilogram.

front: What is the US Merchandise Processing Fee (MPF)?
back: A CBP user fee on imports (19 CFR 24.23). Formal entries pay an ad valorem fee with a per-entry minimum and maximum; informal entries pay a small flat fee. CBP adjusts the amounts every fiscal year; check current values.

front: What is the US Harbor Maintenance Fee (HMF)?
back: An ad valorem fee on imported commercial cargo unloaded at covered US seaports; vessel only, not air, truck or rail; no minimum or cap (19 CFR 24.24). Exports do not pay it (U.S. Shoe, 1998).

front: Do USMCA-originating goods pay the US MPF?
back: No: originating goods properly claimed under USMCA are exempt from MPF (19 CFR 24.23).

front: Is MPF refunded when CBP approves a US post-importation USMCA claim (19 U.S.C. 1520(d))?
back: Yes, with the excess duty. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (Pub. L. 116-260) authorized these MPF refunds, back-dated to 1 July 2020; CBP's earlier no-refund position is superseded.

front: What do the HTSUS rate columns 1-General, 1-Special and 2 mean?
back: 1-General: normal trade relations (MFN) rate. 1-Special: preferential rates under trade programs and FTAs, flagged by program codes. 2: statutory rates for countries without normal trade relations.

front: What is the IGI in Mexico?
back: Impuesto General de Importación: Mexico's general import duty, with rates set by 8-digit fracción arancelaria in the TIGIE and calculated mainly on customs value.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.3

front: How is IVA on a Mexican import calculated?
back: On customs value plus IGI and the other import contributions such as DTA (Ley del IVA art. 27). It is paid on the pedimento and is generally creditable for the importer.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.3

front: How is GST on a commercial import into Canada calculated?
back: CBSA collects it at importation on the value for tax: value for duty plus customs duties and other duties and taxes (excluding GST). GST registrants can generally claim it back as an input tax credit.

front: What is the Harmonized System (HS)?
back: The World Customs Organization's international product nomenclature: the common basis of the US, Canadian and Mexican tariffs and of most countries' trade statistics.

front: How is the HS organized from broadest to narrowest?
back: Sections (groups of chapters), then 2-digit chapters, 4-digit headings and 6-digit subheadings. Example: 8471.30 is chapter 84, heading 84.71, subheading 8471.30.

front: How often is the HS amended, and when does the next edition apply?
back: Normally about every five years. The next edition, HS 2028, takes effect 1 January 2028; every item-master classification must be checked against the correlation tables and remapped where its subheading changes.

front: How many digits is a US HTSUS number and what do they mean?
back: Ten: the 8-digit subheading is the legal tariff line where the duty rate is set; the last 2 digits are a statistical suffix used for trade statistics.

front: How is a Canadian tariff classification number structured?
back: Ten digits: 6 HS digits plus 2 Canadian digits form the 8-digit tariff item, where duty rates are set; the last 2 digits are a statistical suffix.

front: How is a Mexican tariff classification code structured?
back: An 8-digit fracción arancelaria in the TIGIE (6 HS + 2 Mexican digits; sets the duty) plus a 2-digit NICO (Número de Identificación Comercial) for commercial identification.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Sections 3.2 and 8.1

front: Does a US 10-digit HTS number carry over to Canada or Mexico?
back: No. Only the first 6 HS digits are harmonized; digits 7-10 are set independently by each country, so each country's code must be classified and maintained separately.

front: What are the General Rules of Interpretation (GRIs)?
back: Six legally binding rules for classifying goods in the HS and national tariffs. They are applied in numerical order; once a rule settles the classification, later rules are not used.

front: What does GRI 1 say?
back: Classification is determined by the terms of the headings and any relevant section or chapter notes. Section and chapter titles are for reference only. Most goods are classified at GRI 1.

front: What does GRI 2(a) cover?
back: Incomplete or unfinished articles that have the essential character of the finished article, and complete articles presented unassembled or disassembled, are classified as the complete, finished article.

front: What does GRI 2(b) cover?
back: A heading's reference to a material or substance includes mixtures or combinations of it with other materials. Goods of more than one material are then classified under GRI 3.

front: What does GRI 3(a) say?
back: When goods are prima facie classifiable under two or more headings, the heading with the most specific description is preferred over headings with a more general description.

front: What does GRI 3(b) say?
back: Mixtures, composite goods and sets put up for retail sale that GRI 3(a) cannot resolve are classified by the material or component that gives them their essential character.

front: What does GRI 3(c) say?
back: When GRI 3(a) and 3(b) cannot decide, classify under the heading that occurs last in numerical order among those that equally merit consideration.

front: What does GRI 4 say?
back: Goods that cannot be classified under GRIs 1 to 3 are classified under the heading for the goods to which they are most akin. It is rarely used.

front: What does GRI 5 cover?
back: Containers. 5(a): specially shaped cases suitable for long-term use (e.g., camera or instrument cases) presented with their articles classify with them. 5(b): normal packing classifies with the goods unless clearly suitable for repetitive use.

front: What does GRI 6 say?
back: Subheadings are determined by their terms and any subheading notes, applying GRIs 1-5 by analogy and comparing only subheadings at the same level (one-dash with one-dash).

front: What is the purpose of HTSUS Chapter 98?
back: Special classification provisions, e.g., US goods returned (9801) or articles assembled abroad from US components (9802), which can give duty relief if their conditions and documentation requirements are met.

front: What is the purpose of HTSUS Chapter 99?
back: Temporary legislation, temporary modifications and additional import restrictions, e.g., Section 301 and 232 duties. Chapter 99 numbers are reported in addition to the Chapter 1-97 classification, never on their own.

front: What is CROSS?
back: CBP's Customs Rulings Online Search System (rulings.cbp.gov): a searchable database of CBP Headquarters and New York rulings from 1989 on, cross-referenced to later modifications and revocations.

front: What is a US binding ruling?
back: A written CBP decision under 19 CFR Part 177, normally requested before import, applying the law to a specific described transaction. CBP must follow it until modified or revoked, if the facts given were accurate.

front: Can we rely on a CROSS ruling issued to another importer?
back: Only as guidance. Under 19 CFR 177.9 a ruling covers the transaction it describes, and others should not assume it applies. Confirm the facts match, or request our own ruling.

front: What are the HS Explanatory Notes?
back: The WCO's official interpretation of the HS at the international level, describing each heading's scope, inclusions and exclusions. They are not part of the legal text; the US treats them as persuasive, not binding.

front: What is CARM?
back: CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management: CBSA's system for assessing and collecting duties and taxes on commercial imports. It became the official system of record on 21 October 2024.

front: What is the CARM Client Portal (CCP)?
back: CBSA's online portal where importers register their business, delegate access to customs brokers, enrol in programs such as RPP, post financial security and view statements of account.

front: What replaced the B3 in Canada?
back: The Commercial Accounting Declaration (CAD), from 21 October 2024 under CARM. It replaced the B3-3 coding form and the B2 adjustment request; adjustments are submitted as new versions of the CAD.

front: What account numbers does a business need to import commercial goods into Canada?
back: A 9-digit Business Number (BN) plus an import-export (RM) program account, e.g., 123456789RM0001. Both come from the Canada Revenue Agency; the business then registers in the CARM Client Portal.

front: What are CBSA D-Memoranda?
back: CBSA's departmental memoranda (series D1 to D23) explaining how it applies customs legislation, regulations and policy, e.g., D10 classification, D13 valuation, D17 accounting. They are guidance, not law.

front: What is Release Prior to Payment (RPP) in Canada?
back: A CBSA program that releases goods before duties and taxes are paid, with payment due later on the monthly statement of account. Importers must enrol and post financial security.

front: Can a Canadian importer rely on its customs broker's security for RPP?
back: No. Since the CARM transition ended (20 May 2025), importers must post their own financial security in CARM; without it, duties and taxes are payable at release.

front: What is Canada's reason-to-believe correction obligation?
back: Under Customs Act s. 32.2, an importer with reason to believe an origin, tariff classification or value for duty declaration is incorrect must correct it and pay any duties owing within 90 days after forming that belief.

front: What is a pedimento?
back: Mexico's customs declaration, normally transmitted electronically by the agente aduanal, declaring the goods, tariff code, value, origin, customs regime and taxes paid (e.g., IGI, DTA, IVA). It is the core import record.

front: What is Anexo 22 of Mexico's foreign-trade rules (RGCE)?
back: The instructions for completing the pedimento, including appendices (catalogues) of codes, e.g., customs offices, pedimento keys (A1 = definitive import), regimes and countries, that every pedimento must use.

front: What is the padrón de importadores?
back: Mexico's mandatory importer registry (Ley Aduanera art. 59-IV), managed through SAT. Registration requires an active RFC, a valid e.firma and tax compliance; some goods also need a sector-specific padrón.

front: What is the RFC?
back: Registro Federal de Contribuyentes: Mexico's federal taxpayer ID issued by SAT. The importer's RFC is declared on the pedimento and must be active to stay in the padrón de importadores.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.1

front: What is the e.firma?
back: SAT's advanced electronic signature (formerly FIEL): personal, non-transferable credentials used to sign filings such as padrón requests, broker authorizations and electronic value declarations.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 6.1

front: What is Mexico's foreign-trade single window, and who runs it?
back: The Ventanilla Única de Trámites de Comercio Exterior (VUTCE), run by the ATDT under a decree of 4 May 2026. It replaced SAT's VUCEM, a name the trade still uses (as of Oct 2026)

front: What is the TIGIE?
back: Mexico's import and export tariff schedule, contained in the Ley de los Impuestos Generales de Importación y de Exportación (LIGIE).
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 3.2

front: When did USMCA enter into force?
back: 1 July 2020, replacing NAFTA.

front: What are USMCA's names in each country?
back: USMCA in the US, CUSMA in Canada (Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement) and T-MEC in Mexico (Tratado entre México, Estados Unidos y Canadá). All refer to the same agreement.
source: Customs and Trade Compliance Primer, Section 10.2

front: What are the four USMCA origin criteria (A to D)?
back: A: wholly obtained or produced in the region. B: meets the Annex 4-B product-specific rule using non-originating materials. C: made exclusively from originating materials. D: narrow parts/unassembled-goods case meeting a regional value content test.

front: What is a tariff shift rule of origin?
back: A product-specific rule requiring each non-originating material to change tariff classification (chapter, heading or subheading) through production in the region, e.g., 'a change to heading X from any other heading'.

front: What is the USMCA transaction value formula for regional value content (RVC)?
back: RVC = (TV - VNM) / TV x 100, where TV is the good's transaction value adjusted to exclude international shipping costs and VNM is the value of non-originating materials.

front: What is the USMCA net cost formula for regional value content (RVC)?
back: RVC = (NC - VNM) / NC x 100, where NC is total cost minus sales promotion, marketing, after-sales service, royalty, shipping and packing, and non-allowable interest costs.

front: What is the USMCA de minimis rule?
back: A good can still qualify if non-originating materials that fail the required tariff shift are worth no more than 10% of the good's transaction value or total cost (Art. 4.12), subject to exceptions; textiles use weight.

front: What is accumulation under USMCA?
back: Originating materials from one USMCA country count as originating when used in another, and production by several producers across the region can be combined to meet the origin rules (Art. 4.11).

front: Who may complete a USMCA certification of origin?
back: The importer, the exporter or the producer (USMCA Art. 5.2).

front: Since when has Mexico accepted USMCA certifications completed by the importer?
back: Since 1 January 2024, after its transition period of three years and six months from entry into force.

front: Is there a mandatory form for a USMCA certification of origin?
back: No. Any format works, including an invoice, if it contains the nine minimum data elements in Annex 5-A; electronic signatures are allowed.

front: What are the nine minimum data elements of a USMCA certification of origin?
back: 1 certifier role (importer, exporter or producer); 2 certifier; 3 exporter; 4 producer; 5 importer; 6 description and 6-digit HS classification; 7 origin criterion; 8 blanket period; 9 authorized signature and date.

front: What period can a USMCA blanket certification cover?
back: Multiple shipments of identical goods within the period stated on the certification, which may not exceed 12 months.

front: How long must customs accept a USMCA certification of origin?
back: Four years after the date it was completed (USMCA Chapter 5). This acceptance period is separate from the five-year recordkeeping requirement.

front: How does a US importer claim USMCA preference at entry?
back: By holding a valid certification of origin when the claim is made and prefixing the HTSUS number with SPI 'S' on the entry summary. 'S+' is only for certain agricultural goods and textile goods under tariff preference levels.

front: Can a US importer claim USMCA preference after entry if it did not claim at entry?
back: Yes: a post-importation claim under 19 U.S.C. 1520(d) within one year of importation, with a certification of origin. CBP cannot extend the deadline.

front: Under USMCA Art. 34.7, what was due at the sixth-anniversary joint review (1 July 2026)?
back: The Free Trade Commission meets, and each Party confirms in writing whether it wants to extend the 16-year term for another 16 years. Outcome: docs/primers/current-tariff-landscape.md, item V9 (as of Oct 2026)

front: What happens if not every USMCA Party confirms extension at the joint review?
back: The agreement stays in force; the Commission holds annual joint reviews for the rest of the term, and the Parties can still confirm extension. Without it, USMCA terminates 16 years after entry into force (2036).

front: MX: What is the IMMEX program?
back: A Secretaría de Economía program (2006 IMMEX decree) letting a company temporarily import inputs and machinery with import duty (IGI) deferred, to elaborate, transform or repair goods that are then exported.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'industrial' modality?
back: One company carries out an industrial process that elaborates or transforms goods for export under its own program. It is the standard modality for manufacturers.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'controladora de empresas' modality?
back: A certified controlling company integrates the manufacturing operations of one or more controlled companies under a single IMMEX program.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'servicios' modality?
back: Services performed on goods for export, or export services, limited to the activities the Secretaría de Economía lists as eligible.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'albergue' (shelter) modality?
back: One or more foreign companies supply technology and production material to a Mexican shelter company that holds the program, so they manufacture in Mexico without operating their own IMMEX program.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the 'terciarización' (outsourcing) modality?
back: A certified company without its own production facilities has the manufacturing done by third parties (submanufacturers) that it registers in its program (Decreto IMMEX art. 4-V).

front: MX IMMEX: how long can temporarily imported raw materials, parts and components generally stay in Mexico?
back: Generally up to 18 months from import (Ley Aduanera art. 108); the same term covers consumables, packaging and labels. Any longer term for certified companies: the Senior confirms current terms.

front: MX IMMEX: how long can temporarily imported machinery and equipment stay in Mexico?
back: For as long as the IMMEX program remains in force (Ley Aduanera art. 108). It can be changed to definitive import by paying the corresponding duties and taxes.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the legal status of temporary imports not returned or changed to another regime within their term?
back: They are deemed to be in Mexico illegally, because the temporary import regime has ended. IGI, IVA/IEPS with inflation adjustment and surcharges, plus fines, can be assessed; repeated failures put the program at risk.

front: MX IMMEX: what is a 'descargo'?
back: The discharge of a temporary-import balance, recorded when the goods, or the inputs consumed in them, leave Mexico on a return pedimento or change regime. Undischarged balances are duty and tax exposure.

front: MX IMMEX: what is Anexo 24?
back: The RGCE annex setting the minimum content of the automated inventory control system IMMEX companies must keep (Ley Aduanera art. 59-I): temporary imports in, consumption, returns out and balances, available to the authority.

front: MX IMMEX: what is the SCCCyG?
back: SAT's Sistema de Control de Cuentas de Créditos y Garantías: it opens a balance for each temporary import covered by IVA/IEPS certification or a guarantee and reduces it when discharged by export or regime change.

front: MX IMMEX: why do current SAT rules call the SCCCyG annex 'Anexo 30' rather than 'Anexo 31'?
back: The annex was renumbered from 31 to 30 starting with the RGCE for 2022. Industry and some SAT pages still say 'Anexo 31'; cite it as 'Anexo 30 (formerly Anexo 31)' (as of Oct 2026)

front: MX IMMEX: how do Anexo 24 and the SCCCyG depend on each other?
back: Anexo 24 tracks the physical temporary-import inventory; the SCCCyG tracks the VAT credit and guarantee accounts. Discharge reports from the Anexo 24 system feed the SCCCyG, so bad inventory data breaks both.

front: MX IMMEX: what does IVA/IEPS certification give a company?
back: A tax credit equal to the IVA/IEPS on its temporary imports (Ley del IVA art. 28-A, Ley del IEPS art. 15-A), so no cash VAT is paid at import.

front: MX IMMEX: what are the VAT options for an IMMEX company without IVA/IEPS certification?
back: Pay the IVA and any IEPS on each temporary import in cash, or guarantee it with a bond (fianza) or letter of credit in favor of the treasury.

front: MX: What is PROSEC?
back: Programas de Promoción Sectorial: a Secretaría de Economía program letting registered producers in designated sectors import listed inputs and machinery at preferential IGI rates, whether the finished goods are exported or sold in Mexico.
source: Decreto PROSEC (Programas de Promoción Sectorial), DOF 2 August 2002, as amended

front: MX: What is a Regla Octava (Regla 8a) permit?
back: A Secretaría de Economía prior permit, available to PROSEC producers, to import inputs under TIGIE heading 98.02 at the preferential rate, solely for producing goods of the authorized sector.
source: LIGIE article 2, complementary rule 8a (Regla Octava); Secretaría de Economía prior permit

front: US: What is duty drawback?
back: A refund of duties, taxes and fees paid on imported merchandise when that merchandise, a qualifying substitute, or an article made from it is exported or destroyed under CBP supervision (19 U.S.C. 1313).

front: US drawback: what is the maximum refund?
back: 99% of the eligible duties, taxes and fees paid on the designated imported merchandise. The other 1% is not refunded.

front: US drawback: what is the deadline to file a claim?
back: 5 years from the date of importation of the merchandise on which drawback is claimed (19 U.S.C. 1313(r)). The export or destruction must also happen within the 5-year windows set for each type.

front: US drawback: what is 1313(a) manufacturing direct identification drawback?
back: The imported duty-paid merchandise itself is used to manufacture an article that is exported or destroyed. No substitution; use in manufacture within 5 years of import.

front: US drawback: what is 1313(b) manufacturing substitution drawback?
back: Duty-paid imports are designated against exported articles made with other merchandise, imported or domestic, classifiable under the same 8-digit HTS subheading and used within 5 years of the import.

front: US drawback: what is 1313(c) rejected merchandise drawback?
back: Refund on imports that did not conform to sample or specifications, were defective at import, or were shipped without consent, and on retail goods returned for any reason, when exported or destroyed within 5 years of import.

front: US drawback: what is 1313(j)(1) unused merchandise direct identification drawback?
back: The same imported goods are exported or destroyed under CBP supervision within 5 years of import, without being used in the US. Operations such as repacking or testing are not 'use'.

front: US drawback: what is 1313(j)(2) unused merchandise substitution drawback?
back: Refund on an import when other unused goods classifiable under the same 8-digit HTS subheading are exported or destroyed within 5 years of that import.

front: US drawback: what is TFTEA and what did it do to drawback?
back: The Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015. It modernized drawback: 8-digit HTS substitution, uniform 5-year windows and electronic filing. Claims now follow 19 CFR Part 190; legacy claims followed Part 191.

front: US drawback: what is the TFTEA substitution standard for unused merchandise (1313(j)(2))?
back: Same 8-digit HTSUS subheading as the import. If that 8-digit description begins with 'Other', the goods must match at 10 digits; if the 10-digit also begins with 'Other', substitution is not available.

front: US drawback: where and how are claims filed?
back: Electronically in ACE as a drawback entry (entry type 47), with the import entries designated, proof of export or destruction, and any manufacturing records. Usually prepared by a broker or drawback specialist.

front: US drawback: what is accelerated payment?
back: A CBP privilege (19 CFR 190.92) to receive estimated drawback before the claim liquidates. Payment is not liquidation: CBP can still review the claim and recover any overpayment.

front: US drawback: what is a waiver of prior notice?
back: A CBP privilege (19 CFR 190.91) waiving the requirement to notify CBP before exporting or destroying goods for unused (1313(j)) or rejected (1313(c)) claims, so shipments need not wait for CBP's examination decision.

front: US drawback: how long must records supporting a claim be kept?
back: Until 3 years after liquidation of the drawback claim, or longer if another law requires (19 CFR 190.15).

front: US drawback: which additional duties can never be refunded through drawback?
back: Antidumping and countervailing duties (19 U.S.C. 1677h). For other additional duties, check the specific tariff action's terms; see docs/primers/current-tariff-landscape.md.

front: US drawback: how is drawback limited on exports to Canada or Mexico?
back: USMCA rules (19 CFR 182.44) generally cap it at the lesser of US duties paid or duties paid on import into Canada or Mexico. Exceptions (182.45): same-condition goods and Canadian or Mexican originating goods.

front: US: What are the EAR?
back: The Export Administration Regulations (15 CFR Parts 730-774), written and enforced by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), controlling the export, reexport and in-country transfer of commercial and dual-use items, software and technology.

front: US: What is the Commerce Control List (CCL)?
back: Supplement No. 1 to 15 CFR Part 774: the list of items with specific EAR controls, organized into 10 categories and 5 product groups. Each entry is an ECCN with its reasons for control.

front: US export: what do the first two characters of an ECCN such as 3A001 mean?
back: Digit = CCL category, 0-9 (3 = electronics). Letter = product group: A systems, equipment and components, B test and production equipment, C materials, D software, E technology.

front: US export: what do the last three digits of an ECCN signal?
back: Reason for control: 0xx national security, 1xx missile technology, 2xx nuclear nonproliferation, 3xx chemical and biological weapons, 5xx firearms and spacecraft (e.g., 0A501, 9A515), 6xx '600 series' military items, 9xx anti-terrorism, crime control, regional stability, short supply and UN sanctions.

front: US export: what is EAR99?
back: The designation for items subject to the EAR but not on any CCL entry, covering most everyday commercial goods. Usually no license is needed unless the destination, end user or end use triggers one.

front: US export: which four facts drive an EAR license determination?
back: Classification (ECCN or EAR99), destination (Country Chart and embargoes), end user (restricted-party lists) and end use (prohibited uses). 15 CFR Part 732 sets out the steps.

front: US export: under BIS 'Know Your Customer' guidance, what must you do when a transaction shows a red flag?
back: Inquire and resolve it before proceeding; without red flags you may rely on the information received. Examples: buyer evasive about end use; product does not fit the buyer's business; a freight forwarder named as final destination.

front: US export: how do you read the Commerce Country Chart?
back: Take the reasons for control in the item's ECCN (e.g., NS1, AT1), find the destination row in Supplement No. 1 to Part 738. An X under a matching column means a license is required unless a license exception applies.

front: US export: how do OFAC and BIS differ?
back: OFAC (Treasury) administers economic sanctions on countries, regimes and listed persons, such as the SDN List, and covers transactions broadly. BIS (Commerce) controls the items exported under the EAR. A shipment may need both cleared.

front: US export: what is restricted party screening?
back: Checking every party to an export (buyer, consignee, end user, agents) against government lists such as BIS's Entity List and OFAC's SDN List, typically through the Consolidated Screening List.

front: US: What is EEI?
back: Electronic Export Information: export data filed in the Automated Export System (AES) under the Foreign Trade Regulations (15 CFR Part 30), used for trade statistics and export enforcement. It replaced the paper SED.

front: US export: what is ACE AESDirect?
back: The Census Bureau's free web-based tool for filing EEI to AES, reached through an ACE exporter account. Alternatives are AESWebLink, EDI bulk upload or certified third-party software.

front: US export: when is EEI filing generally required?
back: When the value under one Schedule B/HTS number exceeds US$2,500, or at any value when a license is required or another 15 CFR 30.2(a)(1)(iv) category applies (15 CFR 30.2, 30.37(a)).

front: US export: how is the US$2,500 EEI exemption tested?
back: Per Schedule B/HTS number for one USPPI, one consignee and one conveyance: add lines with the same number, and report only numbers over US$2,500, with domestic and foreign origin tested separately.

front: US export: when does a shipment to Canada need EEI?
back: Most US exports to Canada are exempt (15 CFR 30.36), except goods stored in Canada for later export elsewhere, goods moving through Canada to a third country, and 30.2(a)(1)(iv) cases such as license-required goods.

front: US export: what is the ITN?
back: The Internal Transaction Number AES returns when it accepts an EEI filing. The filer gives it to the carrier as proof of filing; exempt shipments carry an exemption legend such as 'NOEEI 30.37(a)'.

front: US export: what is a Schedule B number?
back: A 10-digit Census Bureau export classification based on the HS. EEI can report it or, in most cases, the 10-digit HTSUS import number, except HTS numbers flagged invalid for export.

front: US export: who is the USPPI?
back: The US Principal Party in Interest: the person or entity in the US receiving the primary benefit, monetary or otherwise, from the export, usually the US seller or manufacturer. It answers for the EEI data it supplies.

front: US export: what is a routed export transaction?
back: An export in which the foreign principal party in interest (FPPI) authorizes a US agent, often its forwarder, to file the EEI. The USPPI must still give the agent accurate data and keep records.

front: US export: what are the EEI filing deadlines for vessel and air cargo (non-USML)?
back: Vessel: 24 hours before loading at the US port. Air: 2 hours before scheduled departure (15 CFR 30.4(b)).

front: US export: what are the EEI filing deadlines for truck and rail cargo (non-USML)?
back: Truck: 1 hour before the truck arrives at the US border. Rail: 2 hours before the train arrives at the border (15 CFR 30.4(b)).

front: US export: how long must EEI-supporting records be kept?
back: Five years from the date of export (15 CFR 30.10), by the USPPI, the authorized agent and other parties to the transaction.

front: CA: What is CERS?
back: The Canada Border Services Agency's Canadian Export Reporting System: a free online portal exporters use to file Canadian export declarations. It replaced paper B13A reporting.

front: CA: When must a commercial export from Canada be reported to the CBSA?
back: Generally when going to a country other than the US, Puerto Rico or the US Virgin Islands with a value of CAD 2,000 or more, or when the goods are controlled, regulated or prohibited (Memorandum D20-1-1).

front: CA: What export reporting do most Canadian exports to the US need?
back: None: goods exported for consumption in the US generally need no export declaration; controlled goods present their permit instead. Goods transiting the US to a third country must be reported.

front: MX: What is an export pedimento?
back: The customs declaration an agente aduanal files to export goods from Mexico. For IMMEX companies, the return pedimento is the evidence that discharges temporary imports in Anexo 24 and the SCCCyG.

front: Standard cost: what is a standard cost?
back: A predetermined cost per item (material, freight, duty, overhead) used to value inventory and cost of goods sold, held fixed until the next cost update. Actual costs are compared with it to produce variances.

front: Standard cost: what is a cost roll (rollup)?
back: Calculating each item's total standard by summing its cost elements, and for kits or assemblies its components' costs, into a pending cost that is reviewed before it is posted.

front: Standard cost: what is the difference between a pending and a frozen cost?
back: Pending: a proposed cost from a cost roll that does not yet value anything. Frozen: the current standard used for transactions. Oracle EBS uses these names; Fusion uses cost scenarios [COMPANY: Oracle EBS or Fusion].

front: Standard cost: what happens to on-hand inventory when a standard cost update posts?
back: It is revalued: on-hand (and in-transit) quantity x (new standard - old standard) is booked to a revaluation account. A big duty change on a high-stock item makes a big adjustment.

front: Standard cost: 1,000 units on hand; the standard rises from $12.00 to $12.90 for higher duty. What is the revaluation?
back: 1,000 x ($12.90 - $12.00) = $900 increase in inventory value, posted to the revaluation account. Finance should get this estimate before approving the update.

front: Standard cost: what is the trade-off in how often standards are updated?
back: Frequent updates keep standards close to actual (smaller PPV, truer margins) but add workload, revaluation noise and control risk. Infrequent updates are stable but let variances grow when duty or freight move.

front: Standard cost: why does every cost update need maker-checker review?
back: A wrong standard instantly misstates inventory value and margins. The maker prepares and documents; the Senior or Manager reviews and signs off before posting, every cycle, including after day 90.

front: Standard cost: what four checks should a reviewer run before approving a cost update?
back: Reconcile item counts and totals to the source; review the largest percent and dollar changes; check zero, blank and new-item costs; compare the revaluation estimate with Finance's expectation.

front: Standard cost: in a tariff action, what does the Standard Cost track own?
back: The $: impact on item landed cost and margin, the Oracle cost update and variance explanation. Research owns the WHAT, handed over in the Tariff-Impact Brief.

front: Standard cost: what is purchase price variance (PPV)?
back: (Actual purchase price - standard price) x quantity received. Under standard costing it is recognized at receipt and shows how much more or less we paid than standard.

front: Standard cost: under the usual sign convention, what does a positive PPV mean?
back: Unfavorable: we paid more than standard. A negative PPV is favorable. Confirm how our reports sign it [COMPANY: PPV sign convention], because some reports flip the sign.

front: Standard cost: standard $10.00, PO price $10.40, 500 units received. What is the PPV?
back: (10.40 - 10.00) x 500 = $200 unfavorable (positive PPV): we paid $200 more than standard for this receipt.

front: Standard cost: what are common root causes of PPV for an importer?
back: Supplier price or FX changes; freight or duty changes, such as a new tariff action; and stale or mis-keyed standards, including unit-of-measure errors.

front: Standard cost: why does a new tariff hit margins before standards are updated?
back: Actual landed cost rises at entry, but inventory and COGS stay at the old standard, so the extra duty lands in variance accounts. Until standards and prices change, reported margins absorb it.

front: Landed cost: what is landed cost?
back: The total cost to get an item into our warehouse: purchase price + international freight and insurance + duties and customs fees + brokerage and inland freight.

front: Landed cost (US): why is an ad valorem duty not calculated on landed cost?
back: US duty is a percentage of customs value (transaction value), which excludes international freight and insurance, and the duty itself. Landed cost adds those on top, so duty is not rate x landed cost.

front: Landed cost (US): FOB price $10,000, ocean freight $1,200, duty 25% ad valorem. What are the duty and landed cost before fees?
back: Duty = 25% x $10,000 = $2,500, because international freight is excluded from US customs value. Landed cost before fees = $10,000 + $1,200 + $2,500 = $13,700.

front: Landed cost (MX): price $10,000, freight to the border $1,200, IGI 25%. What is the IGI?
back: 25% x $11,200 = $2,800, because Mexico's customs value includes freight and insurance to the point of entry. DTA and IVA come on top of this.

front: Landed cost: how should freight be allocated to items?
back: By a documented driver that matches what drives the cost, such as weight or cubic volume, applied consistently. The choice shifts cost between heavy, cheap items and light, expensive ones.

front: Landed cost: why can't a cost model use only the HTS base (column 1) duty rate?
back: Additional Chapter 99 duties, USMCA preference, exclusions and AD/CVD can change the effective rate. Research's Tariff-Impact Brief supplies the applicable rate stack per item and origin.

front: Landed cost: an item sells for $20.00 with a $14.00 landed standard. A new 10% duty applies on its $10.00 customs value. What happens to margin?
back: Duty adds $1.00, so landed cost is $15.00. Gross margin falls from $6.00 (30%) to $5.00 (25%) unless the price changes.

front: Incoterms: what are the Incoterms 2020 rules?
back: The ICC's 11 standard trade terms, in effect since 1 January 2020. They allocate delivery, risk transfer, carriage, insurance and export/import clearance between seller and buyer. They do not set price or title transfer.

front: Incoterms 2020: under EXW, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The buyer pays everything from the seller's premises: loading, export clearance, main carriage, insurance, import clearance and duties. The seller only makes the goods available.

front: Incoterms 2020: under FCA, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The buyer. The seller clears export and hands the goods to the buyer's carrier at the named place, where risk passes. FCA suits any transport mode, including containers.

front: Incoterms 2020: under FOB, who pays ocean freight and import duty?
back: The buyer. The seller clears export and loads the goods on board at the named port of shipment, where risk passes. FOB is for sea and inland waterway transport only.

front: Incoterms 2020: under CIF, who pays ocean freight, insurance and import duty?
back: Seller pays ocean freight and insurance to the destination port; buyer pays import clearance and duty. Sea and inland waterway only.

front: Incoterms 2020: under CIF, what minimum insurance cover must the seller buy?
back: Minimum cover under Institute Cargo Clauses (C), unless the parties agree otherwise. CIP, by contrast, requires broader Clauses (A) cover.

front: Incoterms 2020: under CIF, where does risk pass from seller to buyer?
back: When the goods are on board the vessel at the port of shipment, even though the seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port.

front: Incoterms 2020: under DAP, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The seller pays carriage and bears risk to the named destination, goods ready for unloading. The buyer unloads, clears import and pays duties and taxes.

front: Incoterms 2020: under DDP, who pays main freight and import duty?
back: The seller pays everything to the named destination, including import clearance, duties and taxes. Risky where a foreign seller cannot act as importer.

front: Incoterms 2020: why does ICC advise FCA instead of FOB for container shipments?
back: Under FOB, risk passes only when goods are on board, but the seller loses control of a container at the terminal before loading. FCA passes risk at handover to the carrier.

front: Incoterms: why do they matter for landed and standard cost data?
back: They show which costs are already in the supplier price (freight under CIF or DAP) and which we add (freight under FOB or FCA; duty unless DDP), avoiding double counts or gaps.

front: Incoterms (US): if we buy CIF, why isn't the CIF price our US customs value?
back: US transaction value excludes international freight and insurance. A CIF price includes them, so the identified freight and insurance are deducted. FOB and FCA prices normally exclude them already.

front: Tariff action (US): how is a new additional duty built into the HTSUS?
back: Through new Chapter 99 headings and US notes listing covered HTS codes, rates and exceptions. The entry reports the Chapter 99 number together with the Chapter 1-97 classification.

front: Tariff action (US): what does 'stacking' mean?
back: More than one additional duty applying to the same goods, each reported with its own Chapter 99 number on top of the base rate. Each action states whether it stacks with, or is excluded by, others.

front: Tariff action (US): which event usually decides whether a new duty applies to a shipment?
back: Entry for consumption, or withdrawal from warehouse for consumption, on or after the stated date and time (often 12:01 a.m. ET). Not the order, ship or arrival date, unless the action says otherwise.

front: Tariff action (US): why can a new duty hit goods already sitting in a US bonded warehouse?
back: Warehoused goods pay the rate in effect when they are withdrawn for consumption, not when they entered the warehouse (19 CFR 141.69).

front: Tariff action (US): what is an in-transit provision?
back: An exception for goods already loaded and in transit on the final mode of transport before the effective time, if entered by a stated later deadline. Terms differ by action and are claimed with a specific Chapter 99 number.

front: Tariff action (US): what is a product exclusion?
back: A product-specific carve-out from an additional duty, granted through a process defined by that action (e.g., USTR exclusions under Section 301). It has an exact description, dates and its own Chapter 99 number.

front: Tariff action (US): what decides whether USMCA-qualifying goods escape a new duty?
back: Only the action's own terms. Some exempt USMCA-qualifying goods, some reduce the rate, some give no relief. Research cites the exact text in the Tariff-Impact Brief.

front: Tariff action (US): where are the filing instructions for a new action published?
back: In CBP CSMS messages, which say which Chapter 99 numbers to report, in what order, from when, and how to claim exceptions. Cite them, with the Federal Register notice, in the brief.

front: Tariff action (US): why can't you model a new additional duty from the HTS code alone?
back: Applicability can also depend on country of origin, USMCA status, metal or other content, exclusions and entry date. The model needs those attributes for each item.

front: Requirement vs specification: what is the difference?
back: A requirement states what the business needs and why, without choosing a solution. A specification states how the solution meets it: fields, rules, screens, interfaces. The business approves requirements; the build team works from specifications.

front: Business, functional and non-functional requirements: one example each.
back: Business: stop overpaying duty on broker entries. Functional: the audit report flags lines whose applied rate differs from the expected rate. Non-functional: the report runs in under 5 minutes and keeps an audit trail.

front: What does MoSCoW stand for in prioritization?
back: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time). Won't-haves are agreed out of scope for now, which is what stops scope creep.

front: MoSCoW: how do you test whether a requirement is really a Must?
back: Ask: if it is missing on go-live day, can we still operate legally and safely, even with a workaround? If a workaround exists, it is a Should, not a Must.

front: What is an acceptance criterion?
back: A specific, testable pass/fail condition a requirement or story must meet before the business accepts it. Write it before the build starts so the tester and the developer read the same target.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

front: What is the Given/When/Then pattern for acceptance criteria?
back: Given a starting context, When an action or event happens, Then an observable result follows. Example: Given a CN-origin item, When a 25% action takes effect, Then entries from the effective date use the new rate.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

front: What is the user story format?
back: As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit], plus acceptance criteria. Example: As a Research BSA, I want rates effective-dated, so that entries before a change keep the old rate.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

front: As-is vs to-be process: what is each and which do you map first?
back: As-is is how the process runs today, workarounds and pain points included. To-be is the designed future process. Map the as-is first: it is the baseline for requirements, gaps and measuring the change.

front: What is a SIPOC?
back: A one-page, high-level process view: Suppliers, Inputs, Process (about 4 to 7 steps), Outputs, Customers. Use it to agree the scope and boundaries of a process before detailed mapping.

front: What do the letters in RACI mean?
back: Responsible: does the work. Accountable: the one person who signs off. Consulted: gives input before (two-way). Informed: told after (one-way). Each task has exactly one A.

front: Maker-checker: what may the maker never do?
back: Approve or release their own work. A second person checks it and records the review; the maker fixes the findings. Our team applies this to every standard cost update and released tariff model, also after day 90.

front: What is a Definition of Ready?
back: The team's checklist a story must meet before work starts, for example: acceptance criteria written, data sources and dependencies known, and small enough to finish in one sprint.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

front: What is a Definition of Done?
back: The team's checklist a story must meet to count as finished, for example: tested against its acceptance criteria, reviewed by a second person (maker-checker), and accepted by the business owner.
source: Jira epic and story template, docs/templates/bsa/07-jira-epic-story.md

front: What is change control?
back: The process to request, assess (impact, risk, effort), approve, schedule and record every change to a system or agreed scope, so nothing reaches production without review and a record.

front: What is UAT (user acceptance testing)?
back: Business users confirm the system supports their real processes with realistic data before go-live. It answers 'can we run the business on it?', not 'does the code work?'.

front: UAT entry criteria: which earlier testing must be complete before UAT starts?
back: System and integration testing passed, with no open critical defects. UAT tests business fit, not whether the code works.

front: UAT entry criteria: besides passed system testing, what must be ready before UAT starts?
back: The build deployed to the UAT environment, test data loaded, and approved test cases with testers available.

front: UAT exit criteria: what must be true of the tests and defects before UAT can close?
back: All planned test cases executed; no open critical or high defects, unless a workaround is formally accepted; every requirement traced to a passed test.

front: UAT exit criteria: what formally closes UAT?
back: Documented sign-off by the business owner, given after the test and defect criteria are met.

front: What is regression testing?
back: Re-running existing tests after a change to confirm that what worked before still works. Needed for every tool change, patch or upgrade, not only for the feature that changed.

front: Defect severity vs priority?
back: Severity is the impact on the business or system. Priority is how soon it must be fixed. A wrong label on a management report can be low severity but high priority before a board meeting.

front: Positive test vs negative test?
back: A positive test uses valid input and expects success. A negative test uses invalid or edge input (blank HTS, end date before start date, duplicate line) and expects a controlled rejection or error message.

front: What is a requirements traceability matrix?
back: A table linking each requirement to its design, test cases and test results. It proves every requirement was built and tested, and shows what a proposed change will affect.

front: What is a parallel run?
back: Running the old and the new process or system side by side on the same inputs and comparing outputs before switching over. It costs effort but proves the new results tie out.
source: Trade Systems, GTM and e2open Primer, Section 6.1

front: What is a data mapping specification?
back: A document mapping each target field to its source field or fields, with the transformation rule, data type, default, validation and owner. Conversion, interfaces and their tests are built from it.

front: What is a crosswalk (value mapping) table?
back: A table translating code values between systems, for example a legacy program code to the target system's USMCA code. Every source value must map to a target value or be explicitly rejected.

front: Data mapping: what is a transformation rule?
back: The logic applied between source and target: reformat, look up, default, concatenate, split or derive. Write it so developer and tester read it the same way, e.g. 'remove dots from the HTS; keep as 10-character text'.

front: What is a system of record?
back: The authoritative source for a data element; every other system reads from it or syncs to it. Ask it for each field you map, e.g. is item origin mastered in Oracle or in the trade system?

front: What is data cleansing before a migration?
back: Finding and fixing source problems (duplicates, missing values, invalid codes, contradictions) before conversion, each with a rule and an owner, so bad data does not move into the new system.

front: How do you prove a data conversion worked?
back: Reconcile source to target: record counts, control totals (such as the sum of standard cost), field-level checks on keys, and record-by-record samples. Explain and sign off every difference.

front: What is cutover?
back: The planned, time-boxed sequence that switches from the old system to the new: data freeze, final conversion, validation, go/no-go decision, go-live. It includes a tested rollback plan.
source: Trade Systems, GTM and e2open Primer, Section 6.1

front: What is hypercare?
back: A defined period right after go-live with extra support: fast defect triage, daily checks of key outputs and quick fixes, before normal support takes over.
source: Trade Systems, GTM and e2open Primer, Section 6.1

front: SQL: INNER JOIN vs LEFT JOIN?
back: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row of the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match. Use LEFT to keep, and count, orphans.

front: SQL: WHERE vs HAVING?
back: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test COUNT or SUM. Example: GROUP BY entry_no, line_no HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 finds duplicate keys.

front: SQL: why can a column alias made in SELECT be used in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?
back: Logical processing order: FROM and WHERE run before SELECT, and ORDER BY runs after it. So the alias does not exist yet when WHERE is evaluated.

front: SQL: the GROUP BY rule for the SELECT list?
back: Every selected column that is not inside an aggregate (SUM, COUNT...) must be in GROUP BY. You get one output row per distinct combination of the GROUP BY columns.

front: SQL: what does a comparison with NULL return?
back: UNKNOWN, not TRUE or FALSE, because NULL means the value is unknown. So column = NULL never matches. Test with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

front: SQL: why does WHERE program_claimed <> 'USMCA' skip lines with no program?
back: For a NULL program_claimed the comparison returns UNKNOWN, and WHERE keeps only TRUE rows. Write WHERE program_claimed IS NULL, or add OR program_claimed IS NULL.

front: SQL: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)?
back: COUNT(*) counts rows, NULLs and duplicates included. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. So COUNT(*) - COUNT(column) is the number of NULLs in that column.

front: SQL: what does COALESCE do?
back: Returns the first argument that is not NULL. COALESCE(LEFT(hts10, 2), 'UNK') labels lines with a missing HTS instead of letting them drop out of a report.

front: SQL: what is a CTE?
back: A common table expression: a temporary named result set defined with WITH and used in one statement. It turns a long query into named steps you can check one at a time.

front: SQL: what is a window function?
back: A function computed over a set of rows related to the current row, defined by OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...). Unlike GROUP BY it keeps every row. Used for ranks, running totals, de-duplication.

front: SQL: how do you keep one row per key when a file was loaded twice?
back: Number the copies with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY the key columns ORDER BY ...) and keep the rows where the number is 1. Then check: clean rows = distinct keys.

front: SQL: you join entry lines to a rate table and the row count goes up. What happened?
back: Join fan-out: the rate table has more than one row per join key, for example two effective-dated periods. Add the missing key or date condition until the count equals the original.

front: SQL: how do you pick the rate in effect on the entry date?
back: Join on the keys AND entry_date BETWEEN effective_from AND effective_to. Then prove exactly one match per line: row count after the join equals row count before.

front: T-SQL: what does 12 / 9 return?
back: 1. Integer divided by integer truncates. Annualize with SUM(x) * 12.0 / 9 so it also works on INT columns such as qty; never SUM(x) * (12 / 9).

front: SQL: why store money as DECIMAL, not FLOAT?
back: FLOAT is an approximate binary type, so sums can drift by fractions of a cent and fail to tie out. DECIMAL(p,s) stores exact decimal values.

front: SQL: why compute a rate as SUM(duty) / SUM(value) rather than AVG(duty / value)?
back: AVG of line ratios weights a $50 line the same as a $50,000 line. The ratio of sums weights by value, which is what an effective duty rate or PPV % means.

front: Data warehouse: fact table vs dimension table?
back: A fact table holds measurable events at a stated grain (entry lines, receipts) with numeric measures and keys. A dimension describes them (item, supplier, date, country) with attributes to filter and group by.

front: What is a star schema?
back: A fact table in the center joined by keys to dimension tables, with dimensions not chained to each other. Simple to query, and the shape Power BI models work best with.

front: What is the grain of a fact table?
back: What one row represents, e.g. one entry line. State it before building anything. Mixing grains, such as a header-level freight amount repeated on each line, double counts when summed.
source: Trade Systems, GTM and e2open Primer, Section 2.3

front: Slowly changing dimension: Type 1 vs Type 2?
back: Type 1 overwrites the old value, so history is lost. Type 2 adds a new row with valid-from and valid-to dates, so old facts keep the value in effect then, such as an item's HTS before a reclassification.

front: Power Query vs DAX: which does what?
back: Power Query (M) imports and shapes data before it reaches the model: clean, merge, set types. DAX calculates on the loaded model: measures and calculated columns. Clean in Power Query, calculate in DAX.

front: Power BI: calculated column vs measure?
back: A calculated column is computed per row at refresh and stored: use it for attributes you slice by. A measure is computed when queried, in the current filter context: use it for totals and ratios.

front: Why must Effective Duty Rate be a DAX measure, not a calculated column?
back: The rate must be total duty divided by total value for whatever is filtered. A per-row rate column summed or averaged gives wrong totals. DIVIDE([Total Duty], [Total Entered Value]) recalculates in every context.

front: Power BI: what is filter context?
back: The set of filters in force when a measure is evaluated: slicers, the visual's rows and columns, page and report filters, spread through relationships. Same measure, different context, different value.

front: DAX: what does CALCULATE do?
back: Evaluates an expression in a modified filter context, adding, replacing or removing filters. Example: CALCULATE([PPV], Receipts[is_outlier] = FALSE()). It also turns row context into filter context.

front: DAX: DIVIDE vs the / operator?
back: DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, alternate) returns BLANK, or the alternate result, when the denominator is zero or blank. The / operator returns Infinity or NaN instead, which shows on visuals. Use DIVIDE for every ratio, such as duty rate or PPV %.

front: Power BI: what relationship cardinality should a dimension-to-fact link have?
back: One-to-many: one item row to many entry lines, filtering in a single direction from dimension to fact. A many-to-many prompt usually means a duplicate key or wrong grain; fix the data first.

front: A Power BI total differs from your SQL total. What do you check first?
back: Filters (visual, page, report, slicers); relationships (inactive, wrong direction, unmatched keys); the measure definition (sum vs average, exclusions); and the refresh date of the data.

front: Power BI: a slicer shows '(Blank)'. What does it usually mean?
back: Some fact rows have a key with no match in the dimension, e.g. an entry line whose item is missing from the item table. Totals include them; fix the data rather than hide the blank.
